entity.name: Rembrandt
entity.description: The painter who turned light itself into emotion. Rembrandt produced roughly 300 paintings, 300 etchings, and hundreds of drawings during the Dutch Golden Age. He went spectacularly bankrupt in 1656 after spending lavishly on art and curiosities, and died in poverty — buried in a rented grave at the Westerkerk.

story.name: Rembrandt
story.description: A miller's son from Leiden conquers Amsterdam as a portrait painter, completes The Night Watch, goes spectacularly bankrupt, and dies in a rented grave — leaving behind 300 paintings and 40 self-portraits.

moments.name: Rembrandt Is Born in Leiden, the Ninth Child of a Miller
moments.subtitle: A baker's grandson and miller's son will become the greatest painter of the Dutch Golden Age
moments.description: On 15 July 1606, Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was born in Leiden in the Dutch Republic, the ninth child of Harmen Gerritszoon van Rijn, a miller, and Neeltgen Willemsdochter van Zuijtbrouck, a baker's daughter. His mother was Catholic and his father belonged to the Dutch Reformed Church — religion would become a central theme in his art. As a boy, Rembrandt attended a Latin school and in 1620 enrolled at the University of Leiden, but his inclination toward painting quickly won out. He apprenticed for three years with Jacob van Swanenburg, then spent six crucial months with the history painter Pieter Lastman in Amsterdam. By 1625, at just nineteen, Rembrandt had opened his own studio in Leiden.

moments.name: Rembrandt Moves to Amsterdam and Becomes the City's Most Sought-After Portrait Painter
moments.subtitle: The young artist from Leiden conquers the richest city in Europe
moments.description: At the end of 1631, Rembrandt moved to Amsterdam, then rapidly expanding as Europe's business and trade capital. He initially lodged with art dealer Hendrick van Uylenburgh and began practicing as a professional portraitist for the first time, with immediate and spectacular success. In 1634, Rembrandt married Hendrick's cousin Saskia van Uylenburgh, the daughter of a former burgomaster of Leeuwarden. That same year he became a citizen of Amsterdam and a member of the local painters' guild. In May 1639, the couple purchased a grand house on Breestraat for 13,000 guilders — a sum whose mortgage would later contribute to Rembrandt's financial ruin. The house, now the Museum Het Rembrandthuis, still stands.

moments.name: Rembrandt Completes The Night Watch, His Largest and Most Famous Painting
moments.subtitle: The same year Rembrandt finishes his masterpiece, his wife Saskia dies of tuberculosis
moments.description: In 1642, Rembrandt completed The Night Watch (formally Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq), a massive group portrait measuring roughly 12 by 14 feet. Commissioned by the civic guard, the painting broke radically with convention: instead of arranging the militiamen in static rows, Rembrandt depicted them in dramatic motion, bathed in theatrical light and shadow. The painting was hung in the banquet hall of the Kloveniersdoelen, the militia headquarters. That same year, Rembrandt's wife Saskia died, probably of tuberculosis, leaving him with their one-year-old son Titus — the only one of their four children to survive infancy. The Night Watch remains the centerpiece of Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum.

moments.name: Rembrandt Declares Insolvency and Auctions Off 363 Items Including Raphael Drawings
moments.subtitle: Lion skins, Roman busts, a bird-of-paradise, and Old Master paintings all go under the hammer
moments.description: In July 1656, Rembrandt declared his insolvency in Amsterdam, voluntarily surrendering his assets under a legal arrangement called cessio bonorum. Years of overspending on art, prints, rare curiosities, and a 13,000-guilder house had left him unable to pay his creditors. Auctions in 1657 and 1658 sold off 363 items, including paintings by Raphael and Giorgione, busts of Roman emperors, two globes, armor, Asian porcelain, two lion skins, and a bird-of-paradise. The prices were disappointing. By February 1658, his house was sold at foreclosure, and the family moved to modest lodgings on the Rozengracht. Remarkably, Rembrandt was permitted to keep his painting tools so he could continue earning income.

moments.name: Rembrandt Dies in Poverty and Is Buried in a Rented Grave at the Westerkerk
moments.subtitle: The greatest Dutch painter outlives both his partner and his only surviving son
moments.description: On 4 October 1669, Rembrandt died in Amsterdam at the age of 63. He had outlived his wife Saskia (died 1642), his partner Hendrickje Stoffels (died circa 1663), and his son Titus (died 1668 at age 27). Rembrandt was buried four days later in a rented grave at the Westerkerk, one of Amsterdam's grand Protestant churches. Despite his financial ruin, Rembrandt had continued to paint masterworks in his final years, including The Jewish Bride and a series of unflinching self-portraits that rank among the most psychologically penetrating works in Western art. His approximately 300 surviving paintings, 300 etchings, and hundreds of drawings ensure his reputation as one of history's greatest visual artists.
